# Interactive Deliverables {#sec-interactive-deliverables}

Every chapter before this one ends in a document: a rendered
report, a PDF, a paper. Most analyses should end there, because a
static report is finished, versioned, and re-runs the same way for
every reader. Some analyses do not end there, because the question
a stakeholder actually has is not 'what happened in this dataset'
but 'what would happen if I changed this filter, this cutoff, this
subgroup', asked again and again by people who are not going to
learn R to ask it. This appendix is reference material for that
second case: when an interactive app is the right deliverable,
what `teal` buys a clinical-trial team that a hand-built app does
not, how to ship an R application with no server at all, and a
sketch of the smallest Shiny app that would serve the running
HF-HOME example.

## Shiny versus a static report {#sec-interactive-deliverables-when}

A [Shiny](https://shiny.posit.co) application
[@chang2024shiny] is an R program that pairs a user interface
(controls: dropdowns, sliders, buttons) with a server function that
reacts to them and redraws its outputs. It is a different kind of
artifact from everything else in this book, and the difference is
not 'more impressive' or 'more modern'; a Shiny app is the right
choice for a narrower set of problems than its popularity suggests,
and the wrong choice is expensive in a specific way: it has to be
hosted, it has to keep working as R and its packages change under
it, and someone has to be paged when it goes down.

The deciding question is not 'would this be nice to explore
interactively' (almost everything would) but 'who re-runs this, how
often, and do they re-run it with different inputs or just read
the same output again'. Three patterns recur:

- **One-time analysis, many static views.** A trial's primary
  analysis is run once, written up, and read many times, by readers
  who all want the same numbers. A rendered report
  (@sec-quarto, @sec-rrtools) is correct here; an app would let
  readers change the eligibility criteria or the covariate set and
  produce a result the SAP (@sec-analysis-plan) never specified,
  which is a cost, not a feature, for a confirmatory analysis.
- **Repeated use by a team, with inputs that genuinely vary.** A
  data safety monitoring board that reviews accruing adverse-event
  rates at each scheduled look, a clinical operations team that
  checks site-level enrollment weekly, or a medical monitor who
  wants to see one patient's full visit history on demand, are
  asking the same kind of question repeatedly with different
  arguments. A dashboard that takes a site, a date range, or a
  patient ID as input and redraws is doing real work a static
  report cannot: nobody is going to render 200 site-specific PDFs
  every Monday.
- **Exploration during development, not for the deliverable.** A
  statistician exploring a new dataset's missingness patterns,
  trying covariate specifications, or checking a model's residuals
  interactively benefits from a UI that need not survive the
  project: `inspectdf`, `DataExplorer`, or even a throwaway Shiny
  app written in twenty minutes and deleted afterward. This use
  never gets handed to a stakeholder, so it does not raise the
  hosting and maintenance questions below; it is simply a tool, the
  same as an interactive debugger.

Only the second pattern usually justifies the cost of a Shiny
deliverable that other people will depend on. Before building one,
ask who maintains it after the analyst who wrote it moves to
another project, which package versions it pins (an app is a
long-lived piece of software, not a one-time script, and inherits
every renv/Docker concern of @sec-renv and @sec-docker), and whether
a parameterized report (@sec-quarto-params) that regenerates a
handful of PDFs on a schedule would answer the same need at a
fraction of the operational cost. A parameterized report that reruns
nightly for each of twelve sites is often a better answer than a
dashboard that twelve people might log into, because the report has
no uptime to monitor and no session state to reason about.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**An interactive app with no maintainer is a liability, not a
deliverable.** A Shiny app silently breaks when a dependency
changes behavior, when a data source's schema shifts, or when the
server it runs on reaches end of life, and unlike a rendered report
sitting in a shared drive, a broken app actively fails in front of
a user who expected it to work. Before shipping one, write down who
owns it, where it runs, and what lockfile or container pins its
package versions, in the same spirit the DMSP of @sec-federal-dmsp
asks you to write down for data. An app with no named owner should
be a report instead.
:::

### Exercise

1. A clinical operations team asks for 'a dashboard' to track
   enrollment. List three questions you would ask before deciding
   whether that means a Shiny app, a parameterized Quarto report
   rendered on a schedule, or a single static chart updated weekly.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
At minimum: *Who looks at it, and how often?* (If it is three people
once a week, a scheduled report email may suffice; if it is thirty
people checking ad hoc throughout the day, an app has a real
audience.) *Do they need to change any input* (a site, a date
range, a cutoff), *or do they always want the same view?* (If the
view never varies, there is no interactivity to build.) *Who owns
it after this project ends*, and is there budget and a plan for
hosting, monitoring, and updating it as packages and data change?
A team with no name for 'who owns the app in six months' has not
yet justified building one.
:::

## `teal`: a standardized framework for clinical-trial apps {#sec-interactive-deliverables-teal}

Building a Shiny app from scratch for every clinical-trial deliverable
repeats the same work across studies: a filter panel that subsets by
treatment arm, site, or a baseline covariate; a table of adverse
events; a Kaplan-Meier curve; a patient profile. `teal`
[@roche2026teal] is a framework, originated within Roche/Genentech's
NEST (Nest-of-Exploratory-Statistical-Tools) initiative and now
maintained as part of the open-source `pharmaverse` (a community
collection of R packages for clinical reporting that work together
on a shared data model), for assembling that kind of app from
reusable modules rather than writing each one by hand. As of this
writing `teal` and its companion module packages (`teal.modules.clinical`
for prebuilt clinical outputs, `teal.widgets`, and related packages)
are active CRAN and GitHub projects under the `insightsengineering`
organization; verify the current release and maintenance status on
CRAN or the project's GitHub page before depending on it in a
production deliverable, since a framework's module coverage and
API change across versions.

The design is display-only here (it is not installed in this book's
environment), but the shape is worth knowing because it generalizes
beyond Roche's own use: a `teal` app is built by calling `init()`
with a set of ADaM-like datasets (`CDISCFilterableTeal`, mirroring
the ADaM data structures introduced in @sec-cdisc) and a list of
*modules*, each a self-contained analysis view (a summary table, a
Kaplan-Meier plot, an adverse-event listing) that all share a common
filter panel built once by the framework.

```r
library(teal)
library(teal.modules.clinical)
# display-only: teal and its module packages are not installed
# here; this sketch shows the shape of the API, not a runnable app

app <- init(
  data = cdisc_data(
    ADSL = hf_adsl,   # subject-level analysis dataset
    ADAE = hf_adae     # adverse-event analysis dataset
  ),
  modules = modules(
    tm_t_summary(label = "Baseline characteristics",
                 dataname = "ADSL"),
    tm_g_km(label = "Time to event",
            dataname = "ADSL"),
    tm_t_events(label = "Adverse events",
                dataname = "ADAE")
  )
)

shinyApp(app$ui, app$server)
```

The value `teal` adds over a bespoke app is standardization across
studies rather than any single feature: every `teal` app built this
way gives its reviewers the same filter panel, the same navigation,
and modules whose statistical content (which Kaplan-Meier estimator,
which adverse-event grading) has been reviewed once and reused
everywhere, rather than re-implemented, and re-reviewed, per study.
That is the same argument @sec-communicating-table1 makes for `gtsummary` over a
hand-rolled table function, one level up: a shared, validated
building block beats a bespoke one whenever more than one project
will use it. The cost is the same as any framework dependency: a
`teal` app inherits the framework's release cycle, and a module that
does not exist for your analysis still has to be written by hand,
inside the framework's extension points, which has its own learning
curve.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Before adopting `teal` for a deliverable, build the smallest
possible app with one module against synthetic data (HF-HOME
serves well here), and confirm that a colleague unfamiliar with the
framework can open it, apply a filter, and correctly describe what
changed. A framework whose standardized filter panel nobody on the
review team understands has traded one kind of unfamiliarity for
another.
:::

## Running R in the browser: `shinylive` and webR {#sec-interactive-deliverables-shinylive}

A Shiny app ordinarily needs an R process running somewhere: a
server the team operates, or a hosting service such as Posit
Connect or shinyapps.io, which runs the R code and streams updates
to the browser over a persistent connection. `shinylive`
[@posit2024shinylive] removes that requirement by compiling R itself
to WebAssembly through the webR project, and shipping the app's
code and the R runtime together as static files that any web server
(including GitHub Pages, with no R process anywhere) can host. The
browser becomes both the client and the server: there is no
backend to provision, patch, or pay for, and no user ever shares a
session with another user's data, because each browser tab runs its
own private R interpreter.

```r
# display-only: shinylive and webR are not installed in this
# book's environment; this shows the deployment step, not a chunk
# meant to execute here
install.packages("shinylive")
shinylive::export(appdir = "hf_dashboard", destdir = "docs")
# docs/ is now a static site: push it to GitHub Pages, or open
# docs/index.html locally, with no R server anywhere
```

The tradeoff is real and worth stating plainly rather than treating
`shinylive` as a strictly better Shiny:

| Consideration | Server-based Shiny | `shinylive` (webR) |
|---|---|---|
| Hosting cost | A running server (or a paid hosting tier) | A static file host, often free |
| First load | Fast; only the app's own assets download | Slower; the browser downloads an R runtime and package binaries first |
| Data privacy | Data can stay server-side, never sent to the client | Any data the app uses ships to the browser, in the client's memory |
| Package availability | Any CRAN or GitHub package the server can install | Limited to packages built for the webR WebAssembly repository, and some packages do not build at all (compiled code with system dependencies is the usual blocker) |
| Concurrency | One server handles many users; load is shared and must be provisioned for | Each user's browser does its own computing; no shared server to overload |
| Offline use | Needs a live connection to the server | Works fully offline once the page has loaded |

: Shiny hosting tradeoffs: a running server versus `shinylive`'s
WebAssembly build. {#tbl-shinylive-tradeoffs}

The data-privacy row deserves emphasis for clinical work
specifically: because a `shinylive` app runs entirely in the
browser, whatever dataset it loads is present, unencrypted, in that
browser's memory and in the downloaded app bundle if the data is
bundled rather than fetched at runtime. A `shinylive` deployment of
a dashboard over participant-level clinical data defeats the
access controls @sec-federal and @sec-deident spend two chapters
establishing, because anyone who can reach the static files can
extract the data the app ships with. `shinylive` is well suited to
a public demonstration built on synthetic or already-public data
(a teaching app built on HF-HOME's synthetic records, for instance,
or a published paper's de-identified summary results), and poorly
suited to anything that needs the server-side access control a
real clinical dashboard requires.

### Exercise

2. A biostatistician wants to share an interactive exploration of a
   trial's *synthetic* pilot data with collaborators who have no R
   installed and no access to the production Shiny server. Is
   `shinylive` a reasonable choice here, and what would make it a
   bad one?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
Yes, for synthetic data with no server to host it on: the
collaborators need only a browser, the data is already not
sensitive, and the slower first load is a one-time cost worth
paying for zero hosting burden. It becomes a bad choice the moment
the underlying data is swapped for real participant data without
re-examining the privacy row of @tbl-shinylive-tradeoffs, or if any
package the exploration depends on (a compiled survival-analysis
package with system dependencies, say) is unavailable in the webR
package repository, in which case the export silently falls back to
a missing feature rather than failing loudly, and that gap has to be
caught by testing the exported app directly, not inferred from the
server-based version working.
:::

## A minimal sketch: HF-HOME enrollment and outcomes {#sec-interactive-deliverables-sketch}

The smallest Shiny app worth building for a trial like HF-HOME is
one that answers the two questions a clinical operations team asks
repeatedly: how is enrollment tracking against target, and how does
the primary outcome compare between arms so far. The sketch below
is a complete, minimal `app.R` in the classic single-file Shiny
layout. It is display-only: this book's environment does not have
an interactive Shiny session to render it in, so treat the code as
a model to adapt, and verify it by running it locally
(`shiny::runApp()`) against the real HF-HOME CSVs the rest of the
book reads from `analysis/data/raw_data/hfhome/`.

```r
# display-only: no interactive Shiny session in this book's
# rendering environment; run locally with shiny::runApp()
library(shiny)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome")
read_hf <- function(file) {
  readr::read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, file),
                  col_types = readr::cols(patient_id = "c",
                                          .default = "?"))
}

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("HF-HOME: enrollment and outcome monitor"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      dateRangeInput("window", "Enrollment window",
                     start = "2026-01-01", end = Sys.Date()),
      helpText("Outcome summary uses all randomized patients;",
               "it does not depend on the date filter.")
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("enroll_plot"),
      tableOutput("outcome_table")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  hf_rand <- read_hf("randomization.csv")
  hf_outcomes <- read_hf("outcomes.csv")

  enroll_in_window <- reactive({
    hf_rand |>
      filter(rand_date >= input$window[1],
             rand_date <= input$window[2]) |>
      arrange(rand_date) |>
      mutate(cumulative_n = row_number())
  })

  output$enroll_plot <- renderPlot({
    ggplot(enroll_in_window(), aes(rand_date, cumulative_n)) +
      geom_step() +
      labs(x = "Randomization date", y = "Cumulative enrolled",
           title = "Enrollment over time") +
      theme_minimal()
  })

  output$outcome_table <- renderTable({
    hf_rand |>
      left_join(hf_outcomes, by = "patient_id") |>
      group_by(arm) |>
      summarize(n = n(),
                events = sum(event_30d == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
                risk = round(mean(event_30d, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
                .groups = "drop")
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```

Three design choices in this sketch generalize beyond HF-HOME.
First, the app reads data at session start (outside `server()`'s
reactive code, at the top of the function), not inside a
`reactive()` or an input handler, because the randomization and
outcome files do not change while the dashboard is open; re-reading
them on every filter change would be wasted work and, for a file
read over a network mount, a visible delay on every interaction.
Second, the outcome table is deliberately *not* filtered by the
date-range input: the enrollment chart answers 'are we on pace',
the outcome table answers 'what does the primary comparison look
like so far', and conflating them, by applying the same date filter
to both, would make a partial outcome look like it respects the
same cutoff as the SAP's windows when it does not. Decide
deliberately which outputs a given input should touch, and say so
in the UI (the `helpText()` call above exists for that reason), the
same discipline @sec-analysis-plan asks of a SAP's own eligibility
and timing rules. Third, the app never recomputes the primary
analysis of @sec-analysis-plan-worked: a monitoring dashboard built
for an active trial reports accruing data, not the locked, adjusted
primary estimate, and a reviewer who mistakes one for the other
will draw an unblinded conclusion from a view that was never meant
to support one. Where a dashboard like this runs during an active
trial, who may see unblinded arm-level event counts is a governance
decision (consult a data monitoring committee charter), not a
Shiny configuration choice.

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
Use a model to draft the UI and server scaffolding for a dashboard
like this one, not to decide what it is safe to show.

> **Context.** I am building a Shiny app over trial data with
> columns X, Y, Z (attach a data dictionary, not real data). The
> dashboard should let a clinical operations team filter by site
> and date range and see enrollment counts.
>
> **Constraints.** Read data once at session start, not inside a
> reactive expression. Keep any outcome comparison by randomized
> arm un-filtered by the operational date-range input, and label
> why in the UI. Do not add any input or output that would reveal
> unblinded arm-level results to a role this app is not approved
> for.
>
> **Criteria.** The server function contains no inline SQL or raw
> file paths outside one configuration block; every `reactive()`
> depends only on inputs that should trigger recomputation.

*Failure mode.* A model asked only for 'a dashboard with filters'
will happily filter every output by every input, including an
unblinded event-rate table that a clinical operations team may not
be approved to see, because it has no notion of your trial's
governance structure. *Check.* Walk through every output against
the access list in your data monitoring plan before deploying, not
after; the model can write the reactive wiring, but only the
protocol and the charter say who is allowed to see what.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **Match the deliverable to who re-runs it.** A result read many
   times by many people, with the same inputs, is a report; a
   result re-run repeatedly with different inputs by a defined
   team is an app. Most clinical deliverables are the first.
2. **An app is long-lived software, not a script.** It needs a
   named owner, a pinned environment (@sec-renv, @sec-docker), and
   a plan for what happens when a dependency breaks it.
3. **`shinylive` trades a server for a privacy boundary.** Use it
   for public or synthetic data; a `shinylive` app ships its data
   to the browser, so it is the wrong tool for participant-level
   clinical data under access control.
4. **A monitoring dashboard is not the locked analysis.** Keep
   accruing, unlocked views visibly separate from the pre-specified
   primary estimate of @sec-analysis-plan, and respect blinding in
   what each role is shown.

## Cheat sheet

| Task | Tool | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Decide app versus report | Who re-runs it, how often, with what varying inputs | A one-time read is a report, not an app |
| Standardized clinical-trial app | `teal` + `teal.modules.clinical` | Verify current maintenance status before depending on it |
| No-server deployment | `shinylive::export()` | Data ships to the browser; unsuited to participant-level clinical data |
| R and Shiny in WebAssembly | webR, via `shinylive` | Package availability is limited to the webR repository |
| Read data once, not per interaction | Load outside `reactive()`, at the top of `server()` | Avoids redundant reads on every filter change |
| Separate monitoring from the locked analysis | Distinct outputs, distinct access, clear labeling | Protects blinding and the SAP's pre-specification |

: Interactive deliverables at a glance. {#tbl-interactive-cheat-sheet}
